name: Electrohomeopathy

lead: Electrohomeopathy is a system of alternative medicine created by the Italian count Cesare Mattei in the 19th century. It holds that disease stems from disordered 'electrical' fluids in the blood and lymph, and uses colour-coded plant preparations called electroids, said to restore balance.

Its link to appearance is by claim: Mattei's colour scheme assigned a blue series of remedies to skin ailments. Scientific reviewers examined the remedies as early as 1892 and have not found support for the system's mechanisms.

paras: Practitioners prescribe diluted herbal liquids or globules, taken by mouth or applied to the skin, matched to the colour-coded remedy series (red, green, white, yellow, blue). It is mainly practiced in India and Pakistan.

Medical critics say the remedies have no demonstrated effect beyond placebo, and that relying on them in place of treatment can delay care for serious disease. Ingredients are undisclosed and unstandardized, and India does not recognize it as a healthcare discipline.

chain: Colour-coded plant remedies taken or applied
angle.text: Practitioners present the blue-coded series as a remedy for skin ailments, and people who follow the system use it hoping to clear skin complaints. This is a claimed route only; the system's mechanisms have not been demonstrated in studies.

lead: Electrohomeopathy, also called electropathy, is a system of alternative medicine devised by Count Cesare Mattei (1809-1896), a nobleman from near Bologna, Italy. It combines homeopathic-style dilution with the idea that plant remedies carry a restorative 'electrical' quality, and it was promoted in the late 19th century as a treatment for conditions including cancer.[1][2]

In the context of appearance, its relevance lies in its skin-oriented claims: Mattei's colour system associated blue remedies with skin ailments, and modern practitioners in South Asia offer plant preparations for skin and hair complaints.[1] Proponents describe the remedies as non-toxic and selective in action.[1]

Medical reviewers have assessed the system critically since its early years. An 1892 British committee examined the remedies and the patients treated, and analysis of the preparations found nothing beyond distilled water, according to Wikipedia's account; medical critics have classed it as quackery.[2] No peer-reviewed clinical studies of its therapeutic claims are known.

paras: Mattei held that diseases arise from imbalances in the body's electrical fluids, carried in the blood and lymph, and that each illness had a plant-derived cure. Remedies were made by fermenting and distilling herbal mixtures whose composition was kept secret, and were grouped by colour: red for blood disorders, green for digestive complaints, white for nervous conditions, yellow for glandular problems and blue for skin ailments.[1] Wikipedia describes the system as blending humoral theory and modified Hahnemann homeopathy, with remedies said to be fixed with 'electrical' force.[2]

Mattei retired to the Apennines around 1859 and built the Rocchetta Mattei castle, where he developed his remedies; by the early 1870s he was producing labelled phials.[1] Disciples including Theodor Krause in Germany spread the system, a consortium was set up in Regensburg in the early 1880s, and a priest, Father Muller, is reported to have brought it to India in the late 1870s.[1] London's St Saviour's Cancer Hospital experimented with it from 1873.[1]

In 1892 an inquiry led by Morell Mackenzie, prompted by a challenge from W. T. Stead, followed five breast cancer patients whose tumours progressed; the committee called the system unadulterated quackery.[2] A British Medical Journal piece the same year was titled 'Matteism: An Exposure'.[1] Mattei died in 1896; Krauss later expanded the line, introducing injectable forms.[1][2] A 2008 symposium in Bologna marked the bicentenary of his birth.[2]
The system survives mainly in India and Pakistan. India does not recognize it as a healthcare discipline, and it has been called quackery there.[2]
No studies found. The only systematic examination on record is the 1892 committee inquiry described above, which reported no benefit.[2]

Critics note that the preparations are unstandardized, and the 1890s medical press reported patient harm from impure distillates.[1] The broader concern raised by clinicians is delayed treatment of serious illness.[2]
